questions.question: Increasing the number of CPUs and the amount of memory on an existing virtual machine is an example of what?

options.why: Correct. You are making one resource bigger.
A bigger VM is still one instance.

questions.explanation: Changing the size of a single resource is vertical scaling.

questions.question: Adding more virtual machine instances to handle increased traffic is an example of what?

options.why: Scaling up increases the size of a resource.
Predictability is a benefit, not a scaling action.

questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scale out) adds more instances.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about scalability in the cloud are true?

options.text: You can increase resources when demand increases
Once you scale up, you can never scale down
options.why: You can scale down or in when demand falls.

options.text: You only pay for the resources you are using
Scaling always requires buying new physical servers

questions.explanation: Cloud scalability works in both directions and costs follow what you use.

questions.scenario: A web app keeps each user's shopping cart in the memory of the web server. The team plans to scale out to 10 instances.
questions.question: What problem is most likely?

options.text: Users may lose their carts when requests go to a different instance
options.why: Correct. In-memory state is not shared across instances.

options.text: The app will automatically become read-only

options.why: Azure allows scaling; the issue is app design.

options.text: The SLA will drop to zero
options.why: SLAs are unrelated to this design flaw.

questions.explanation: Scale-out works best with stateless apps; store session state in a shared cache or database.
